course.title: Trigonometry
course.description: From side ratios in right triangles to the unit circle, repeating graphs, identities and the vector and wave problems they solve.
course.audience: A capable adult who knows right-triangle distances and similar shapes from Discere's geometry course and can rearrange simple formulas.

paragraphs: When a right triangle is enlarged, its sides grow but its angles stay the same, and the sides keep the same proportions to one another. The shorter leg of a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 is 0.6 of the hypotenuse, and it is 0.6 of the hypotenuse in a triangle ten times the size. Trigonometry is the study of this fixed link between the angles of a triangle and the ratios of its sides, and the three main ratios have names of their own: the sine, the cosine and the tangent. Because the angle alone fixes each ratio, one measured angle and one measured length are enough to find a height, a distance or another angle that cannot be measured directly.

The same ratios describe more than triangles. Put an angle at the centre of a circle of radius 1 and its cosine and sine become the coordinates of a point on the rim, for any angle at all, including angles beyond a quarter turn and beyond a full turn. As the angle turns, the height of that point rises and falls in a smooth repeating wave, and the same wave describes a rider on a Ferris wheel, the hours of daylight through a year and the rise and fall of the tide. The same ratios also split a force or a journey into two parts at right angles, and the parts of several forces or journeys can then be added whatever directions they point in.

Trigonometry has a reputation for formulas to be memorised, yet nearly all of them come from two pictures, the right triangle and the circle of radius 1, and most can be rebuilt from a sketch when they are needed. Working with the subject is mostly a matter of reading a situation, deciding which ratio or which angle it involves, and checking the answer against the picture.
outcomes: You'll be able to find sides and angles of any triangle.
You'll be able to read exact values for 30, 45 and 60 degrees and work in radians.
You'll be able to read any angle's sine and cosine from the unit circle.
You'll be able to read and fit amplitude, period, shift and midline for a repeating quantity.
You'll be able to solve basic trigonometric equations and use the main identities.
You'll be able to resolve vectors into components and combine waves.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Geometry: Shape and Space, Maths Foundations.

modules.title: Triangles and their ratios
modules.description: Ratios that survive scaling, solving right triangles, exact values and triangles with no right angle.

modules.title: Circles and waves
modules.description: Radians, the unit circle and the graphs that repeat.

modules.title: Identities, equations and uses
modules.description: Relationships that always hold, solving with them, and trig applied to vectors and sums of waves.

concepts.title: Sine, cosine, tangent
concepts.summary: For an acute angle in a right triangle: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent.

concepts.title: Why ratios are fixed
concepts.summary: Similar triangles have equal side ratios, so the ratios depend only on the angle.

concepts.title: Find a side
concepts.summary: Choose the ratio that links the known and wanted sides, then multiply or divide.

concepts.title: Inverse functions
concepts.summary: arcsin, arccos and arctan return the angle from a ratio.

concepts.title: Special triangles
concepts.summary: Half a square gives 45-45-90 with sides 1, 1, sqrt 2. Half an equilateral triangle gives 30-60-90 with sides 1, sqrt 3, 2.

concepts.title: Exact values
concepts.summary: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = sqrt2/2, sin 60 = sqrt3/2; cos is the same read backwards; tan 45 = 1, tan 60 = sqrt 3.

concepts.title: Law of cosines
concepts.summary: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C: Pythagoras with a correction for the angle between a and b.

concepts.title: Law of sines
concepts.summary: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C.

concepts.title: Radian
concepts.summary: The angle at the centre of a circle that subtends an arc equal to the radius; 2 pi radians make a full turn.

concepts.title: Arc and sector
concepts.summary: Arc length s = r theta and sector area A = 1/2 r^2 theta, with theta in radians.

concepts.title: Unit circle
concepts.summary: The point at angle theta on the circle of radius 1 is (cos theta, sin theta).

concepts.title: Reference angle
concepts.summary: The acute angle to the x-axis; the trig values match it up to sign.

concepts.title: Amplitude and period
concepts.summary: y = A sin(Bx): amplitude A, period 2 pi / B.

concepts.title: Shift and midline
concepts.summary: y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D shifts right by C and moves the midline to D.

concepts.title: Fit a periodic model
concepts.summary: From the maximum, minimum and period: A = (max - min)/2, D = (max + min)/2, B = 2 pi / period.

concepts.title: Use the model
concepts.summary: Evaluate it at a time, or solve for the time when it reaches a value.

concepts.title: Pythagorean identity
concepts.summary: sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1, because (cos, sin) lies on the unit circle.

concepts.title: Angle formulas
concepts.summary: sin(a + b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b; sin 2a = 2 sin a cos a; cos 2a = 1 - 2 sin^2 a.

concepts.title: Two solutions per cycle
concepts.summary: sin x = c has solutions at x and pi - x in each cycle; cos x = c has x and 2 pi - x.

concepts.title: Rewrite then solve
concepts.summary: Use identities or factoring to make one function equal to a constant.

concepts.title: Components
concepts.summary: A vector of size V at angle theta has V cos theta along the axis and V sin theta across it.

concepts.title: Bearing
concepts.summary: A direction measured clockwise from north; east displacement = d sin(bearing), north = d cos(bearing).

concepts.title: Single wave form
concepts.summary: a cos x + b sin x = R cos(x - phi), with R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and tan phi = b/a.

concepts.title: Same-frequency sums
concepts.summary: Two sinusoids of the same frequency always add to a sinusoid of that frequency.

lessons.title: Ratios that survive scaling
lessons.orientation: Define sine, cosine and tangent as ratios of the sides of a right triangle, and find a ratio from a given triangle.
lessons.nextAction: Use a known angle and one known side to find an unknown side, and use a known ratio to find an unknown angle.

blocks.text: A right triangle with legs 3 and 4 has a hypotenuse of 5, so its shorter leg is 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6 of the hypotenuse, its longer leg is 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 of it, and the shorter leg is 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75 of the longer one. Each of these numbers compares two sides of the same triangle, and together they describe its *shape*, how steeply it rises compared with how far it runs.

**Trigonometry** is the study of how the angles of a triangle fix ratios of this kind. If the angle at one corner determines these three numbers, then knowing that angle and one side of a right triangle is enough to find the other sides without measuring them, and knowing two sides is enough to find the angle.

diagram.alt: Two right triangles drawn to the same scale, one with legs 3 and 4 and hypotenuse 5, the other with legs 6 and 8 and hypotenuse 10. Beside each are three ratios of its sides: 0.6, 0.8 and 0.75 for both.
diagram.caption: Both triangles give the same three ratios, although the second has sides twice as long. Use the buttons to switch triangles.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the sides of a right triangle from a chosen angle and write its sine, cosine and tangent as ratios.
intro.whyItMatters: Every distance you can measure with a ruler can be found indirectly once an angle and one side are known.

reveal.text: The legs became 9 and 12, and 9 ÷ 15 is 0.6, the same as 3 ÷ 5. The next screen shows why enlarging cannot change it.

steps.headline: Enlarging a right triangle changes its sides but not its angles, and when the angles stay the same the ratios between the sides stay the same too.

lead.text: Two triangles are [[similar|Same angles, with every side in the same proportion to its partner. Met in Geometry: Shape and Space.]] when one is an enlargement of the other, and Euclid proved in Book VI of the *Elements*, in Proposition 4, that triangles with equal angles have their sides in proportion. In the figure the smallest triangle has legs 3 and 4, and the other two multiply every side by 2 and by 3, so each keeps the same angle $A$ at its left-hand corner while the sides grow.

diagram.alt: Three right triangles sharing the angle A at the left corner: legs 3 and 4, legs 6 and 8, and legs 9 and 12. Each has the ratio 0.6 for the side opposite A divided by the hypotenuse.
diagram.caption: Each triangle is an enlargement of the one before, so angle A stays the same and the ratio stays at 0.6. Dashed outlines show the smaller triangles.

afterFigure.text: Call the multiplier $k$. The side opposite $A$ becomes $3k$ and the hypotenuse becomes $5k$, so their ratio is $\frac{3k}{5k}$, in which the $k$ cancels and leaves $0.6$. The same cancellation happens for every pair of sides, which is why **a ratio of two sides belongs to the angle and not to the size of the triangle**. Only a change of *angle* can change it, and that is the property the rest of this course builds on.

steps.headline: The words opposite and adjacent depend on which angle you look from, while the hypotenuse is always the side across from the right angle.

lead.text: Look at the 3-4-5 triangle from its left-hand corner, the angle $A$. One leg touches that corner and the other lies across from it. The leg that touches $A$ is called the **adjacent** side, the leg across from $A$ is the **opposite** side, and the remaining side, which lies across from the [[right angle|An angle of 90 degrees, marked by a small square. Met in Geometry: Shape and Space.]], is the **hypotenuse**.

diagram.alt: A right triangle with legs 3 and 4 and hypotenuse 5. Seen from the angle A at the left, the leg of 3 is opposite and the leg of 4 is adjacent. Seen from the angle B at the top, the leg of 4 is opposite and the leg of 3 is adjacent.
diagram.caption: Opposite and adjacent depend on the angle you look from, and the hypotenuse stays where it is. Use the buttons to change the angle.

afterFigure.text: Switch the figure to the angle $B$ at the top and the labels change: the leg of length 4, which was adjacent to $A$, is now opposite $B$, and the leg of length 3 is adjacent to it. *Opposite* and *adjacent* are therefore not properties of a side alone but of a side *and an angle*, so you have to say which angle you are looking from before you use either word. The hypotenuse does not change, because the right angle does not move, and it is kept apart from both words.

reveal.text: The side across from $B$ is the horizontal leg, of length 4, which is the same leg that was adjacent to $A$.

steps.headline: Sine, cosine and tangent are the three ratios of a right triangle's sides, and each is named for the angle it is measured from.

lead.text: Since the ratios depend only on the angle, each deserves a name that mentions the angle. For an acute angle $A$ in a right triangle, $\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ is called the **sine** of $A$, written $\sin A$. The ratio $\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ is the **cosine**, $\cos A$, and $\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ is the **tangent**, $\tan A$.

diagram.alt: The 3-4-5 triangle three times, each highlighting the two sides used by one ratio: sine of A is 3 over 5 or 0.6, cosine of A is 4 over 5 or 0.8, and tangent of A is 3 over 4 or 0.75.
diagram.caption: Each ratio uses two of the three sides, and the highlighted pair changes with the ratio. Use the buttons to compare them.

afterFigure.text: In the 3-4-5 triangle with $A$ at the left, that gives $\sin A = 3/5 = 0.6$, $\cos A = 4/5 = 0.8$ and $\tan A = 3/4 = 0.75$, the same three numbers as in the opening figure. Many people remember the definitions as *SOH CAH TOA*: Sine is Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent is Opposite over Adjacent.

The word *sine* has an odd history. Indian astronomers, among them Aryabhata around the year 499, tabulated the half-chord of an arc under a Sanskrit name, which Arabic writers wrote as *jiba*. By the usual account it was later misread as the Arabic *jayb*, meaning a fold, and Latin translators of the twelfth century rendered that as *sinus*, the source of our word.

steps.headline: Find the sine of the angle opposite the side of length 8 in a right triangle with legs 8 and 15.

workedSteps.text: The hypotenuse is not given, so find it with Pythagoras' theorem: the squares of the legs add to the square of the hypotenuse.
The square root of 289 is 17, so the three sides are 8, 15 and 17.
The angle asked about lies across from the side of length 8, so 8 is the opposite side.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse.

steps.headline: Find the cosine of the other acute angle of that triangle, the one opposite the side of length 15.

workedSteps.text: The sides are still 8, 15 and 17. The new angle lies across from 15, so 15 is now the opposite side, and the leg touching it is the 8.
Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, which for this angle uses the 8.
For the first angle the adjacent side was 15. Work out the cosine of that first angle, the one opposite the side of length 8.

steps.headline: Each angle has one value of sine, cosine and tangent, and a calculator can give it without any triangle being drawn.

lead.text: Since the three ratios belong to the angle, they can be worked out once and looked up afterwards, which is what printed tables did for centuries and what the sin, cos and tan keys of a calculator do now. For an angle of 25° the calculator gives $\sin 25° = 0.423$, $\cos 25° = 0.906$ and $\tan 25° = 0.466$ to three decimals, and these hold for *every* right triangle that has a 25° angle, whether its hypotenuse is 1 centimetre or 1 kilometre.

The calculator must be in degree mode for these values. Angles can also be measured in radians, a unit met in lesson 5, and in radian mode the same key press for $\sin 25$ returns −0.132, which is the sine of a very different angle.

reveal.text: The value is the same for a hypotenuse of any length: a hypotenuse of 10 would make the opposite side 3.42, and the next lesson uses exactly this to find unknown sides.
The missing leg is 8, so this is the 6-8-10 triangle from the opening figure, and its tangent for the angle opposite 6 is 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75, the same as for 3-4-5.

recap.keyIdea: Sine, cosine and tangent are ratios of a right triangle's sides that depend only on the angle, so they are the same for every size of triangle.

blocks.text: You saw that enlarging a right triangle multiplies every side by the same number, which cancels out of any ratio of two sides. The three ratios are named from the point of view of one acute angle, as opposite over hypotenuse for sine, adjacent over hypotenuse for cosine and opposite over adjacent for tangent, and a calculator gives their value for any angle.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns this round: with one side and an angle known, a ratio gives the unknown side, and with two sides known it gives the angle.

lessons.title: Solving right triangles
lessons.orientation: Find a missing side with a ratio and a known angle, and a missing angle with an inverse function.
lessons.nextAction: Work out the exact values of sine, cosine and tangent at 30°, 45° and 60° from two triangles, with no calculator.

blocks.text: In every right triangle with a 35° angle, the side opposite that angle divided by the side next to it is the same number, $\tan 35° = 0.700$, whatever the size of the triangle, so a single angle and a single measured length are enough to find the other sides. A flagpole shows how: standing 20 m from its foot, with an instrument held 1.6 m above the ground and aimed at the top, you read an angle of 35° above the horizontal.

The pole, the ground and the line of sight form a right triangle in which one angle and one side are known, and the height to be found is the side opposite the angle. The instrument is 1.6 m above the ground, so the triangle gives the height above that level, and the 1.6 m below it has to be added at the end.

diagram.alt: A flagpole on level ground with an observer 20 metres away whose eye is 1.6 metres above the ground. The line of sight to the top makes an angle of 35 degrees with the horizontal. The height above eye level is unknown.
diagram.caption: The line of sight, the horizontal and the pole form a right triangle with a known angle and a known side. Use the buttons to add the height of the eye.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find a missing side or angle of a right triangle, choosing the ratio from the two sides involved.
intro.whyItMatters: Heights, slopes and distances that cannot be measured directly can be found from one angle and one length.

reveal.text: The opposite side is 20 × 0.700 = 14.0 m. The next screen turns this working into a method that applies to any known side.

steps.headline: To find a side, write the ratio that contains the side you know and the side you want, and rearrange it for the unknown.

lead.text: In the flagpole triangle the two sides concerned were the adjacent and the opposite, and the ratio that joins those is the tangent, so $\tan 35° = \frac{\text{opposite}}{20}$. Multiplying both sides by 20 isolates the unknown, giving $\text{opposite} = 20 \tan 35° = 14.0$ m, and because the instrument was held 1.6 m above the ground the flagpole is $14.0 + 1.6 = 15.6$ m tall. The reasoning does not depend on this triangle: you **list the side you know and the side you want, and choose the ratio that contains exactly those two**.

diagram.alt: A right triangle with the angle theta at the left corner, drawn three times. In each, one side is marked as known and one as wanted: adjacent known and opposite wanted gives the tangent, hypotenuse known and opposite wanted gives the sine, hypotenuse known and adjacent wanted gives the cosine.
diagram.caption: The ratio to use is the one that contains the known side and the wanted side. Use the buttons to see the three pairings.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the three pairings for an angle $\theta$. When the legs are involved the tangent links them, when the hypotenuse is known and the opposite side wanted the sine does, and when the hypotenuse is known and the adjacent side wanted the cosine does. It is a *mistake* to reach for the same ratio every time, because a sine equation that leaves out one of the two sides in the problem cannot be solved for the other.

When the wanted side is the one underneath, the rearrangement divides instead of multiplying: from $\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ you get $\text{hypotenuse} = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\sin\theta}$.

steps.headline: A kite string 50 m long makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal. Find how high the kite is above the hand, and how far it is along the ground.

workedSteps.text: The string is the hypotenuse, since it lies across from the right angle. The height is the side opposite the 40° angle.
The known side is the hypotenuse and the wanted side is the opposite, so the ratio that contains both is the sine.
Multiply by 50 and evaluate with the calculator in degree mode.
The ground distance is the adjacent side, and the pair hypotenuse and adjacent calls for the cosine.

steps.headline: Use the same kite to check the horizontal distance by a different route.

workedSteps.text: The 50 m string, the height 32.1 m and the ground distance form the same right triangle.
Pythagoras gives ground² = 2500 − 1030.4, which is about 1469.6, and so the ground distance is about 38.3 m, matching the cosine result.
The angle between the string and the ground is 40°. Use the cosine of 40° to find the ground distance from a string of 70 m.

reveal.text: When the unknown is the hypotenuse it sits under the line: rope = 12 ÷ sin 50°. Multiplying instead gives 9.2 m, shorter than the pole, which cannot happen for a hypotenuse.

steps.headline: When two sides are known, their ratio is a number, and an inverse function turns that number back into the angle.

lead.text: A ramp rises 1.2 m over a run of 10 m, and you want the angle it makes with the ground. The rise is the opposite side and the run is the adjacent side, so the tangent of the angle is $\frac{1.2}{10} = 0.12$. That fixes a value of the tangent but not yet the angle, and the calculator answers the missing step with the **inverse tangent**, written $\tan^{-1}$ or *arctan*, which returns the angle whose tangent is the number you give it.

diagram.alt: Two right triangles with two sides known and the angle unknown. The ramp rises 1.2 metres over a run of 10 metres, giving an angle of about 6.84 degrees. The flagpole triangle has 14 metres opposite and 20 metres adjacent, giving about 35 degrees.
diagram.caption: With two sides known, their ratio is a tangent, and the inverse tangent turns it back into an angle. The ramp is drawn to scale. Use the buttons to compare the cases.

cases.label: The flagpole
cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360"><defs><marker id="anpole" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><polygon class="f-sunken s-line w1" points="40,310 340,310 340,100"/><line class="s-ink w3" x1="340" y1="310" x2="340" y2="100"/><line class="s-ink w3" x1="40" y1="310" x2="340" y2="310"/><line class="s-ink w3" x1="40" y1="310" x2="340" y2="100"/><polyline class="f-none s-ink w1" points="326,310 326,296 340,296"/><polyline class="f-none s-warn w2" points="84,310 84,308.9 83.9,307.8 83.9,306.6 83.8,305.5 83.6,304.4 83.5,303.3 83.3,302.2 83.1,301.1 82.9,300 82.6,298.9 82.3,297.8 82,296.8 81.6,295.7 81.2,294.7 80.8,293.6 80.4,292.6 79.9,291.6 79.5,290.5 79,289.5 78.4,288.6 77.9,287.6 77.3,286.6 76.7,285.7 76,284.8"/><text class="t-bold t-warn" x="97.2" y="297" text-anchor="middle">θ</text><text class="t" x="352" y="210" text-anchor="start">14 m</text><text class="t" x="190" y="336" text-anchor="middle">20 m</text><text class="t-bold" x="410" y="120" text-anchor="start">The flagpole triangle</text><text class="t" x="410" y="160" text-anchor="start">tan θ = 14 ÷ 20 = 0.7</text><text class="t-bold t-accent" x="410" y="200" text-anchor="start">arctan 0.7 ≈ 35.0°</text></svg>

afterFigure.text: Here $\theta = \arctan 0.12 \approx 6.84°$, a gentle slope, as the ramp drawn to scale shows. The same works for any ratio: the angle whose sine is a given number is the **inverse sine** $\sin^{-1}$, and the angle whose cosine it is, the **inverse cosine** $\cos^{-1}$. The flagpole triangle shows that the process undoes the earlier one, since $\arctan(14 \div 20) = \arctan 0.7 \approx 35.0°$ returns the angle that was used to find the 14.

reveal.text: The rise and run are the opposite and adjacent sides, so tan θ = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6, and arctan 0.6 ≈ 31.0°.

steps.headline: The −1 in sin⁻¹ marks an inverse function, which returns an angle, and it is not the reciprocal, which would return another ratio.

lead.text: It is natural to read $\sin^{-1} x$ as $\frac{1}{\sin x}$, since the same notation on numbers means a reciprocal, but on a calculator key it means something else. The key $\sin^{-1}$ takes a ratio and returns an *angle*: $\sin^{-1} 0.5 = 30°$. The reciprocal $\frac{1}{\sin 30°}$ is a different number, $\frac{1}{0.5} = 2$, which is a ratio and not an angle, and it has a name of its own, the cosecant, that this course does not need.

Two habits protect you from this error. The first is to ask what kind of thing the answer should be: a missing angle is a number of degrees, and a missing side is a length. The second is to check the mode, since in radian mode $\sin^{-1} 0.6$ shows 0.644 where in degree mode it shows 36.9, and **the same key gives different numbers in the two modes**.

reveal.text: The inverse sine gives 53.1°, and the reciprocal 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25 is a ratio. The 53.1° angle belongs with the 3-4-5 triangle of lesson 1, whose angle has sine 0.8.

steps.headline: Three quick checks catch most errors: the hypotenuse is longest, a small angle has a short opposite side, and sine and cosine stay below 1.

lead.text: The 15.66 m rope was longer than its 12 m pole because the rope is the hypotenuse, and the 9.2 m that comes from multiplying 12 by $\sin 50°$ instead of dividing by it is ruled out by the same fact, since it would make the rope shorter than the pole. The check works for angles too. A leg is always shorter than the hypotenuse, so the sine or cosine of an acute angle is a number between 0 and 1, and a result of 1.25 in an angle problem shows that a reciprocal was taken somewhere. A small angle has a short opposite side, so the 6.84° ramp should rise only a little over its run, and it does: 1.2 m over 10 m.
These checks take seconds, and they catch the two errors this lesson has described, a ratio chosen from the wrong pair of sides and a calculator in the wrong mode.

reveal.text: The 30 m is the adjacent side, so the height above the eye is 30 tan 40° ≈ 25.2 m, and adding the eye height gives 26.7 m, the same two-part method as the flagpole.

recap.keyIdea: Choose the ratio that contains the side you know and the side you want, rearrange it for the unknown, and use an inverse function when the angle is the unknown.

blocks.text: You found sides by multiplying a known side by the ratio that links it to the wanted one, and by dividing when the wanted side sat underneath, as the hypotenuse does. You found angles with the inverse functions, which return an angle where the reciprocal would return a ratio, and you checked each answer against the facts that the hypotenuse is longest and that sine and cosine of an acute angle lie between 0 and 1.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows that three angles, 30°, 45° and 60°, have ratios that can be written exactly, and derives them from a square and an equilateral triangle.

lessons.title: Angles with exact answers
lessons.orientation: Derive exact values of sine, cosine and tangent for 30°, 45° and 60° from two triangles, and use them to solve a triangle exactly.
lessons.nextAction: Find sides and angles of triangles with no right angle, using the law of cosines and the law of sines.

blocks.text: A calculator reports $\sin 45°$ as 0.7071067811865476, a number whose digits never settle into a pattern, and yet the same value can be written exactly with a few symbols. A square of side 1 shows how: its diagonal cuts it into two right triangles whose acute angles are both 45°, and Pythagoras' theorem gives the length of that diagonal, so the sine of 45° can be read as a ratio of two exact lengths with no rounded decimal anywhere in it.

A second shape, the equilateral triangle, gives 30° and 60° in the same way, and those three angles, which turn up constantly in geometry and engineering, are the ones whose ratios can be read exactly from a drawing.

diagram.alt: A square of side 1 with its diagonal of length root 2, and then one half of the square as a right triangle with legs 1 and 1, hypotenuse root 2, and two angles of 45 degrees.
diagram.caption: The diagonal of a unit square has length √2 and cuts the square into two identical right triangles. Use the buttons to see one triangle alone.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to draw the two special triangles and read from them the exact sine, cosine and tangent of 30°, 45° and 60°.
intro.whyItMatters: Exact values keep a calculation free of rounding until the last step.

reveal.text: The squares of the legs add to 1 + 1 = 2, so the hypotenuse squared is 2 and the hypotenuse is √2, about 1.41. That is longer than one leg and shorter than the two together, and it is the diagonal of the unit square in the opening figure.

steps.headline: A square cut along its diagonal gives a triangle whose angles and sides fix the sine, cosine and tangent of 45° exactly.

lead.text: Take the half-square from the opening. Its two legs are equal, so the angles opposite them are equal, and since the angles of a triangle add to 180° and one of them is 90°, the other two share 90° and are 45° each. The hypotenuse satisfies $h^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 = 2$, so $h = \sqrt2$, a number that is neither a whole number nor a fraction and whose decimal never ends. A root of this kind that cannot be simplified away is called a **surd**, and a value written with one is an **exact value**, as opposed to the rounded decimal that a calculator displays.

diagram.alt: A 45-45-90 right triangle with legs 1 and 1 and hypotenuse root 2, giving sine and cosine of 45 degrees as root 2 over 2 and tangent as 1. A second view scales it to hypotenuse 10, with legs 5 root 2, about 7.07.
diagram.caption: Every 45-45-90 triangle has these ratios, so the same values give the legs when the hypotenuse is 10. Use the buttons to compare the sizes.

afterFigure.text: Reading the ratios from the angle at the left gives $\sin 45° = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\cos 45° = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\tan 45° = \frac11 = 1$. Multiplying the top and bottom of $\frac1{\sqrt2}$ by $\sqrt2$ gives the equivalent form $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$, which is the one usually written. Sine and cosine agree because *both legs are equal*, and tangent is 1 for the same reason. Since the ratios belong to the angle, they hold for every 45-45-90 triangle, including the one with hypotenuse 10 in the second view, whose legs are $10 \times \frac{\sqrt2}{2} = 5\sqrt2$.

steps.headline: Find the legs of a 45-45-90 triangle whose hypotenuse is 10, first exactly and then as a decimal.

workedSteps.text: Each leg is opposite a 45° angle and the hypotenuse is known, so the ratio that contains them is the sine.
Multiply by 10 and substitute the exact value of sin 45°.
The two acute angles are both 45°, so the other leg is equal and needs no separate calculation.
For a length you can measure, evaluate the surd with a calculator.
As a check, the squares of the legs should add to the square of the hypotenuse.

reveal.text: The sine of 60° is 0.866, not 1, because sine is not proportional to the angle. The next screen shows where 0.866 comes from exactly.

steps.headline: An equilateral triangle cut in half gives a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, √3 and 2, and from it the ratios for 30° and 60°.

lead.text: A second triangle gives the other two angles. An equilateral triangle of side 2 has three angles of 60°, and its height, drawn from the top to the middle of the base, cuts it into two identical right triangles. Each has a hypotenuse of 2, a base of 1 and angles of 60° at the base and 30° at the top, because the height halves the top angle. The height $h$ then satisfies $1^2 + h^2 = 2^2$, so $h = \sqrt3$.

diagram.alt: An equilateral triangle of side 2 with its height drawn, giving two right triangles. One half has a base of 1, a height of root 3, a hypotenuse of 2 and angles of 30, 60 and 90 degrees.
diagram.caption: Cutting an equilateral triangle in half gives a right triangle with sides 1, √3 and 2. Use the buttons to see the whole triangle and its half.

afterFigure.text: From the 30° angle at the top, the opposite side is 1, the adjacent side is $\sqrt3$ and the hypotenuse is 2, so $\sin 30° = \frac12$, $\cos 30° = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\tan 30° = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{3}$. From the 60° angle at the base the sides trade roles, so $\sin 60° = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $\cos 60° = \frac12$ and $\tan 60° = \sqrt3$. **The sine and cosine swap** between the two angles, because the side opposite one acute angle is adjacent to the other.
This also settles the guess in the previous question: $\sin 60° = 0.866$ against $\sin 30° = 0.5$, a ratio of about 1.73 and not 2, since sine is not proportional to the angle.

steps.headline: The nine exact values come from two triangles that you can draw from memory, so the table does not need to be learnt by rote.

lead.text: The figure collects the values for 30°, 45° and 60°. Each entry is a ratio of two sides of a triangle with sides $1, 1, \sqrt2$ or $1, \sqrt3, 2$, and it is exact, which means a surd such as $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the value itself and its decimal 0.866 is a rounded copy. If the table slips from memory, a sketch of the two triangles recovers every entry in under a minute, and the sketch also tells you which side is opposite and which adjacent, so errors of the kind in the swap are visible at once.

A few patterns help as checks. The sines of 30°, 45° and 60° increase, 0.5, 0.707 and 0.866, while the cosines decrease through the same three numbers; and tangent passes through 1 at 45°, where opposite and adjacent are equal.

diagram.alt: A table of sine, cosine and tangent for 30, 45 and 60 degrees. The exact view gives 1/2, root 3 over 2 and root 3 over 3 for 30 degrees; root 2 over 2, root 2 over 2 and 1 for 45 degrees; root 3 over 2, 1/2 and root 3 for 60 degrees. The other view gives the rounded decimals.
diagram.caption: Every entry comes from one of the two triangles. Use the buttons to switch between exact values and decimals.

reveal.text: The angles 30° and 60° add to 90°, and the side opposite one is adjacent to the other, so cos 60° = sin 30° = 1/2.

steps.headline: Find both legs of a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 6, exactly and then to two decimals.

workedSteps.text: The shorter leg is opposite the 30° angle, and the hypotenuse is known, so use the sine.
The longer leg is opposite the 60° angle, so use sin 60°, which is the same value as cos 30°.
Evaluate the surd for the decimal length of the longer leg, to two decimal places.

steps.headline: Keep exact values through a calculation and round once at the end, because rounding early lets small errors accumulate.

lead.text: Exact values also check themselves. Squaring and adding the sine and cosine of 45° gives $\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2 = \frac12 + \frac12 = 1$ exactly, while the rounded decimals give $0.7071^2 + 0.7071^2 = 0.99998$, which is close to 1 but not equal to it. The exact version shows a relation that the rounded one hides, and lesson 9 will show that the relation holds for every angle.
The practical rule is that a length meant for a ruler is evaluated at the last step, as the 5√2 ≈ 7.07 was, and everything before that stays in surds.

reveal.text: The exact height is 12 × √3/3 = 4√3, which is about 6.93 m, and the ratio itself came from the table without a calculator.

recap.keyIdea: Two triangles, the half-square with sides 1, 1 and √2 and the half-equilateral with sides 1, √3 and 2, give exact values of sine, cosine and tangent at 30°, 45° and 60°.

blocks.text: You derived the values of the table from the two triangles with Pythagoras' theorem, which gives √2 for the diagonal of a unit square and √3 for the height of an equilateral triangle of side 2. Sine and cosine swap between 30° and 60° because the opposite side of one angle is the adjacent side of the other, and the exact surds are kept until a length is needed.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson drops the right angle, and uses two laws that relate the sides and angles of any triangle.

lessons.title: Triangles with no right angle
lessons.orientation: Choose between the law of cosines and the law of sines from the given parts, solve a triangle, and find its area from two sides and the angle between them.
lessons.nextAction: Measure angles in radians, so that arc length and sector area need no conversion factor.

blocks.text: Two sides of a triangle measure 7 and 10 metres and the angle between them is 60°. If that angle were a right angle, Pythagoras' theorem would give a third side of $\sqrt{149}$, about 12.21, but at 60° the triangle has no right angle and the theorem does not apply. The third side is still fixed by the two lengths and the angle, since nothing else is free to vary, and there must therefore be a rule that turns those three numbers into a fourth.

The triangles of the earlier lessons had a right angle supplied for free, but a triangle marked out between three points on the ground almost never does, and its sides and angles are tied together all the same, so that measuring some of them fixes the rest. A rule for the missing side of the 7 and 10 triangle is therefore the first step towards solving any triangle from the parts that were measured.

diagram.alt: Two triangles with sides 7 and 10 meeting at a vertex. With a right angle between them the third side is root 149, about 12.21. With a 60 degree angle between them the third side is not yet known.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose the law of cosines or the law of sines from what is given, solve a triangle, and find its area without a height.
intro.whyItMatters: Any triangle that you can measure with two lengths and an angle can be solved without drawing it.

reveal.text: Narrowing the angle pulls the ends of the two sides closer together, so the third side shrinks, and the next screen finds that it becomes 8.89.

steps.headline: The law of cosines finds the third side from two sides and the angle between them, and it reduces to Pythagoras' theorem when that angle is 90°.

lead.text: Pythagoras' theorem needs a right angle, and a height can create one. From the vertex opposite the side $a$, drop a perpendicular of length $h$ onto $a$, which splits the triangle into two right triangles. In the left one, $h = b\sin C$ and the foot of the height lies $b\cos C$ from the corner $C$, so it lies $a - b\cos C$ from the other end. Pythagoras' theorem in the right-hand triangle then reads $c^2 = h^2 + (a - b\cos C)^2$.

diagram.alt: A triangle with sides a, b and c and the angle C between a and b. A perpendicular height h from the opposite vertex meets the side a at D, splitting a into b cos C and a minus b cos C. A second view uses a equal to 7, b equal to 10 and C equal to 60 degrees, giving h about 8.66, CD equal to 5 and DB equal to 2.

afterFigure.text: Multiplying out the bracket gives $c^2 = h^2 + a^2 - 2ab\cos C + b^2\cos^2 C$, and the left-hand triangle says $b^2 = h^2 + b^2\cos^2 C$, so the two terms $h^2$ and $b^2\cos^2 C$ together make $b^2$. What remains is the **law of cosines**, $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$.

With the numbers of the figure, $c^2 = 49 + 100 - 140\cos 60° = 149 - 70 = 79$, so $c = 8.89$. If $C$ were $90°$ the cosine would be 0 and the last term would vanish, leaving $c^2 = a^2 + b^2$, so *Pythagoras' theorem is the special case* of the law in which the angle is a right angle.

steps.headline: Two sides of a triangle are 5 and 8, and the angle between them is 50°. Find the third side.

workedSteps.text: The known parts are two sides and the angle between them, so the law of cosines gives the third side directly.
Substitute a = 5, b = 8 and C = 50°. The angle must be the one between the two sides, because it is opposite the side being found.
Evaluate with the calculator in degree mode, remembering that cos 50° ≈ 0.6428.
Take the square root.

steps.headline: The law of sines says that every side divided by the sine of the angle opposite it gives the same number, which links two sides to their opposite angles.

lead.text: The same height gives a second law. In the figure the height $h$ from the vertex above $D$ can be written from the left-hand right triangle as $h = b\sin C$, and from the right-hand one as $h = c\sin B$. Both are the same length, so $b\sin C = c\sin B$, and dividing both sides by $\sin B \sin C$ gives $\frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$.

diagram.alt: The triangle with its height h from vertex A. In the left right triangle the height equals b times sine of C. In the right-hand right triangle it equals c times sine of B. Both expressions give the same height.
diagram.caption: The same height can be written from either side of it. Use the buttons to read each right triangle.

afterFigure.text: Dropping the height from a different vertex gives the same relation for the remaining pair, and together they make the **law of sines**: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$. Each side is paired with the angle across from it, as in lesson 1, and the constant ratio is the same for all three pairs.

The law needs one complete pair, a side and the angle opposite it, to start from. With two angles known, the third follows from the fact that the angles add to 180°, and then a single known side supplies the pair.

steps.headline: A triangle has A = 40°, B = 60° and a = 10. Find the side b.

workedSteps.text: The side a is opposite A and the side b is opposite B, so the known pair is a with A, and the wanted side pairs with B.
workedSteps.math: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B

workedSteps.text: Substitute the known values.
Multiply both sides by sin 60° to isolate b.
Evaluate with the calculator in degree mode.

steps.headline: The given parts decide the law: cosines for two sides with their angle or for three sides, sines when a side and its opposite angle are known.

lead.text: Every problem begins by listing what is known. With two sides and the angle between them, nothing is known in pairs, so the law of cosines finds the third side. With three sides, the law of cosines rearranged as $\cos C = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$ gives an angle. With two angles and a side, the angle sum gives the third angle, and the law of sines finds a second side from the pair that you hold.

The law of sines does *not* solve every triangle, as the first and second cases show, because with no complete pair it has nothing to start from. The fourth case, two sides and an angle that is not between them, does give a pair, but it has a complication that the next screen describes.

diagram.alt: A triangle with sides a, b, c and angles A, B, C, shown four times with the known parts in green and the wanted part in blue. Two sides and the included angle: law of cosines for the third side. Three sides: law of cosines for an angle. Two angles and a side: law of sines. Two sides and an angle not between them: law of sines, which may have two answers.
diagram.caption: What you are given decides the law. Use the buttons to compare four common cases.

reveal.text: The cosine of the angle opposite 6 is (16 + 25 − 36) ÷ 40 = 0.125, so the angle is 82.8°, only slightly more than a right angle.

steps.headline: Two sides and an angle that is not between them can fit two different triangles, because an angle and its supplement have the same sine.

lead.text: Take $A = 30°$, $a = 7$ and $b = 10$. The law of sines gives $\sin B = \frac{b\sin A}{a} = \frac{10 \times 0.5}{7} = 0.714$, and the calculator's inverse sine returns $B = 45.6°$. That is not the only angle with this sine: an angle and the angle that makes it up to 180°, called its **supplement**, have equal sines, and $180° - 45.6° = 134.4°$ has sine 0.714 too, a fact that lesson 6 explains with the unit circle. Since $30° + 134.4° = 164.4°$ is below 180°, this second angle leaves room for a triangle as well.

The figure shows both. The side of 7 is shorter than the 10, and it can swing down to the base at two points, giving $c = 13.56$ in one triangle and $c = 3.76$ in the other. **The data do not decide between them**, which is why this arrangement of parts is called the ambiguous case. When the side opposite the given angle is long enough, only one triangle fits, and a sketch is the quickest way to see which situation you are in.

diagram.alt: A triangle with a 30 degree angle at the left, a side of 10 from it to the top vertex, and a side of 7 opposite the 30 degree angle. The side of 7 can reach the base at two points, giving one triangle with angle B of about 45.6 degrees and another with angle B of about 134.4 degrees.
diagram.caption: With two sides and a non-included angle, the side of 7 can swing to either of two points on the base. Use the buttons to see each triangle; the dashed line marks the other.

reveal.text: The second triangle has B = 134.4° and C = 15.6°, so the angles still sum to 180°, and its third side is the short 3.76.

steps.headline: The area of a triangle is half the product of two sides and the sine of the angle between them, with no height needed.

lead.text: The familiar area is half the base times the perpendicular height, and the height was exactly what the split of the triangle supplied: with the base $a$, the height is $h = b\sin C$. Substituting gives $\text{area} = \frac12 a\,h = \frac12 ab\sin C$, a formula that needs only two sides and the angle *between* them.

For sides 7 and 10 with $C = 60°$ the area is $\frac12 \times 7 \times 10 \times \sin 60° = 35 \times 0.866 = 30.3$ square units. The perpendicular is never drawn or measured, which is the great convenience when a surveyor knows two distances and an angle and cannot stand at the foot of the height.

reveal.text: The area is ½ × 40 × 55 × sin 75° ≈ 1062.5 m², found without measuring any height.

recap.keyIdea: The law of cosines solves a triangle from two sides and the angle between them, or from three sides, and the law of sines solves it from a side and its opposite angle.

blocks.text: Both laws come from dropping a height, which splits any triangle into two right triangles. The law of cosines, $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$, contains Pythagoras' theorem as its right-angle case, and the law of sines pairs each side with the sine of its opposite angle, with the ambiguous case arising because an angle and its supplement share a sine. The same height gives the area, $\frac12 ab\sin C$.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson changes the unit of angle from degrees to radians, which makes the length of an arc as simple as a product.

lessons.title: Turning in radians
lessons.orientation: Convert between degrees and radians, and use arc length and sector area.
lessons.nextAction: Place a point on a circle of radius 1 and read sine and cosine from its coordinates, for every angle.

blocks.text: A full turn is 360 degrees, a number usually traced to Babylonian astronomers, who counted in sixties, and nothing in a circle itself makes 360 special. The circle does supply a measure of its own: lay the radius along the rim, and the arc it covers makes an angle at the centre, which is the same whether the circle is large or small, since the radius and the rim grow by the same factor.

That angle is called a radian, and measuring angles in it turns the rim into a ruler, so that the length of an arc follows from the radius and the angle by a single multiplication. It is also the unit in which the waves of the sine and cosine take their simplest form.

diagram.alt: Two circles, one of radius 5 cm and one of radius 3 cm, each with an arc along the rim equal in length to the radius. In both, the angle at the centre is the same, one radian, about 57.3 degrees.
diagram.caption: An arc as long as the radius makes the same angle at the centre in a big circle and a small one. Use the buttons to change the radius.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert angles between degrees and radians and use them to find an arc length and a sector area.
intro.whyItMatters: Radians remove the conversion factors from formulas about circles and waves.

reveal.text: The whole rim is 2πr long and each radian takes up r of it, so a full turn is 2π radians, about 6.283.

steps.headline: A radian is the angle at the centre of a circle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius, and it is the same size in every circle.

lead.text: Bend a piece of string as long as a circle's radius along its rim, and the two ends of the string, joined to the centre, make an angle. That angle is called **one radian**. A circle of radius 5 cm and one of radius 3 cm have different strings, but each string is a fixed share of its own circle, so the angle is the same in both, about 57.3°, which the opening figure shows. A measure that comes from the circle itself, and not from a choice like 360, is why mathematicians prefer it.

diagram.alt: A circle with radii drawn at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 radians, so that each rim arc between neighbours is as long as the radius. Six such arcs do not quite close the circle: the remaining 0.283 of a radius brings the total to 2 pi, about 6.283.
diagram.caption: Laying the radius round the rim six times leaves a gap, and the whole rim holds 2π radii. Use the buttons to follow the steps.

afterFigure.text: Laying the radius again and again round the rim marks one radian at each step. Six steps fit with a little rim left over, and the whole rim holds exactly $\frac{2\pi r}{r} = 2\pi$ radii, which is about 6.283. A full turn is therefore $2\pi$ radians, and a half turn is **$\pi$ radians**, the same angle as 180°. Notice that $\pi$ radians is *180 degrees* and not 3.14 degrees: the number 3.14 counts radians, and each radian is a large angle.

steps.headline: Because 180° and π radians are the same half turn, converting multiplies by π/180 in one direction and by 180/π in the other.

lead.text: The equation $180° = \pi$ radians is the only fact needed. Dividing both sides by 180 gives $1° = \frac{\pi}{180}$ radians, which is about 0.01745, and dividing both by $\pi$ gives $1 \text{ radian} = \frac{180°}{\pi}$, which is about 57.3°. To turn degrees into radians you multiply by $\frac{\pi}{180}$, and to turn radians into degrees you multiply by $\frac{180}{\pi}$. Checking which way to go is easy: a number of degrees is larger than the matching number of radians, so converting to degrees must make the number *bigger*.

Many common angles have neat forms in radians. A right angle is $\frac{\pi}{2}$, 60° is $\frac{\pi}{3}$, 45° is $\frac{\pi}{4}$, and 30° is $\frac{\pi}{6}$, and the exact triangles of lesson 3 read the same way: $\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac12$. The $\pi$ is usually left in the answer, and a decimal is given only when a number is needed.

steps.headline: Convert 150° to radians, exactly and as a decimal.

workedSteps.text: Degrees become radians by multiplying by π/180, since 180° is π radians.
Simplify the fraction 150/180 by dividing the top and bottom by 30.
The exact value keeps π.
For a decimal, use π ≈ 3.14159.

steps.headline: Convert 2 radians to degrees.

workedSteps.text: Radians become degrees by multiplying by 180/π.
Evaluate 180 ÷ π, which is about 57.3, and double it. Give the result in degrees to one decimal place.

steps.headline: In radians, arc length is the radius times the angle, and the area of a sector is half the radius squared times the angle.

lead.text: The definition gives the arc at once. One radian cuts off an arc of length $r$, two radians cut off $2r$, and an angle of $\theta$ radians cuts off $s = r\theta$. A sector is the share $\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$ of the whole disc, whose area is $\pi r^2$, so its area is $\frac{\theta}{2\pi} \times \pi r^2 = \frac12 r^2\theta$. With a radius of 5 m and an angle of 1.2 radians, the arc is $5 \times 1.2 = 6$ m and the area is $\frac12 \times 25 \times 1.2 = 15$ m².

diagram.alt: A circle of radius 5 metres with a shaded sector, shown for angles of 1 radian, 2 radians and pi over 2 radians. The arc lengths are 5, 10 and about 7.85 metres, and the areas are 12.5, 25 and about 19.63 square metres.
diagram.caption: Arc length and sector area both grow in step with the angle in radians. Use the buttons to compare three sectors.

afterFigure.text: **Neither formula has a conversion constant**, which is the practical reason for radians. In degrees the arc would be $\frac{\pi r \theta}{180}$, with the $\frac{\pi}{180}$ carried along every time. The figure shows the same circle with three angles, and the arc and area simply scale with the number of radians.

reveal.text: The arc is 8 × 0.75 = 6 m. With the angle already in radians, no conversion is needed.

steps.headline: The formulas s = rθ and A = ½r²θ hold only when θ is in radians, so an angle given in degrees must be converted first.

lead.text: Suppose a sector has radius 5 m and an angle of 60°. Putting 60 straight into $s = r\theta$ gives 300 m, which is longer than the whole circle's rim of $2\pi \times 5 = 31.4$ m, and so cannot be an arc of it. Converting first, $60° = \frac{\pi}{3}$ radians, gives $s = 5 \times \frac{\pi}{3} = 5.24$ m, about a sixth of the rim, as 60° should be. The same check protects against the error: an arc is never longer than the rim, so a result of 300 m signals the wrong unit.

The same formula measures the Earth. One degree of latitude is $\frac{\pi}{180}$ radians, and the Earth's radius is about 6,371 km, so a degree along a meridian is $6371 \times \frac{\pi}{180} = 111.2$ km, close to the 111 km found in atlases, and the distance between two places on one meridian follows from their latitudes.

reveal.text: The arc is 5 × π/3 ≈ 5.24 m. Putting 60 into the formula would have given 300 m, which is longer than the whole rim.
The angle is 80 × π/180 ≈ 1.396 rad, so the area is ½ × 81 × 1.396 ≈ 56.5 cm².

recap.keyIdea: A radian is the angle that cuts off an arc equal to the radius, so 180° is π radians, an arc is rθ and a sector is ½r²θ.

blocks.text: You defined the radian from the circle itself, found that a full turn is 2π radians, and converted with the rule that 180° is π radians. The arc and sector formulas then lose their constants, but they require the angle to be in radians, so an angle given in degrees is converted first.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson places a point on a circle of radius 1, so that an angle of any size, not only an acute one, has a sine and a cosine.

lessons.title: The unit circle
lessons.orientation: Read sine, cosine and tangent of any angle from the unit circle, and use reference angles to reuse the exact values.
lessons.nextAction: Read the amplitude, period, shift and midline of a repeating graph.

blocks.text: In lesson 1 the sine of an angle was the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse, which only makes sense for an acute angle, since a right triangle has no room for an angle of 120°. Yet a bearing of 120° or a wheel turned through 210° are everyday angles, and it is natural to ask for their sines. The way forward is to choose the hypotenuse to be 1. Then $\sin\theta$ is the length of the opposite side and $\cos\theta$ is the length of the adjacent side, so the triangle can be read as the coordinates of a point on a circle of radius 1.

A point on a circle can be placed at any angle, past 90°, past a full turn or even backwards, so the pair of coordinates that gave the ratios of lesson 1 also gives a sine and a cosine for angles that no right triangle could hold.

diagram.alt: A right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and angle theta, whose horizontal side is cosine theta and vertical side is sine theta. In the second view the same triangle sits in a circle of radius 1 centred on the angle, with the far corner on the circle.
diagram.caption: With a hypotenuse of 1 the two legs are the cosine and the sine. Use the buttons to place the triangle in a circle of radius 1.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read the sine, cosine and tangent of any angle from a point on the unit circle, with the right sign.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets one definition cover every angle, including the negative ones and those beyond a full turn.

reveal.text: After a half turn the point is on the opposite side of the circle, at (−1, 0), so its x coordinate is −1. The next screen shows that this x coordinate is the cosine of 180°.

steps.headline: The point at angle θ on the unit circle is (cos θ, sin θ): the x value is the cosine and the y value is the sine.

lead.text: The **unit circle** is the circle of radius 1 centred at the origin, and angles are measured from the positive x-axis, turning counterclockwise. Take the point $P$ on it at angle $\theta$ and drop a perpendicular onto the x-axis. That makes a right triangle with hypotenuse 1, exactly as in the opening, whose horizontal side is $\cos\theta$ and whose vertical side is $\sin\theta$, and so $P = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. At 40° the point is about $(0.766, 0.643)$ and at 70° it is $(0.342, 0.940)$, so as the angle grows the point climbs and its x value shrinks.

diagram.alt: The unit circle with a point P at an angle of 40 degrees and at 70 degrees. The x coordinate of P is the cosine of the angle and the y coordinate is the sine. At 40 degrees P is about (0.766, 0.643) and at 70 degrees about (0.342, 0.940).
diagram.caption: The point's x value is the cosine and its y value is the sine. Use the buttons to move the point from 40° to 70°.

afterFigure.text: This gives a new reading of the old ratios: **the x value is the cosine and the y value is the sine**. The tangent stays $\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, the y value divided by the x value, which is the slope of the line from the origin to $P$. Nothing in the definition needs the angle to be below 90°, since the point exists at every angle, and that is how sine and cosine are extended past the right triangle.

steps.headline: Moving the point past 90° gives sine and cosine for every angle, and their signs are the signs of y and x in the quadrant the point reaches.

lead.text: At 90° the point is at the top, $(0, 1)$, and as the angle grows further it goes on round into the second quadrant, where its x value is negative. The two axes cut the plane into four **quadrants**, numbered counterclockwise from the first, where $x$ and $y$ are both positive. At 120° the point is $(-0.5, 0.866)$, the mirror image of the point at 60° across the y-axis, with the same height and the opposite x value. Sine and cosine are therefore defined for *every* angle, and a negative value only says that the point lies to the left of, or below, the axes. The **signs** are not facts to memorise: they are the signs of $x$ and $y$ in each quadrant, which you can read from the picture.

afterFigure.text: The figure also shows 210°, in the third quadrant, where both coordinates are negative, and 300°, in the fourth, where only $y$ is. Tangent, as $y \div x$, is positive in the first and third quadrants, where the two coordinates share a sign, and negative in the second and fourth, which is why $\tan 135°$ cannot be positive.

reveal.text: The mirror across the y-axis keeps the height and reverses the x value, so the point at 135° is (−0.707, 0.707) and cos 135° = −0.707.

steps.headline: A reference angle is the acute angle between the radius and the x-axis, and it gives the size of sine and cosine for any angle.

lead.text: Every point on the circle is the mirror image, across one of the axes, of a point in the first quadrant, so its coordinates have the same sizes as that point's and differ only in sign. The acute angle that the radius makes with the x-axis is called the **reference angle**, and it is the angle you look up. In the second quadrant it is $180° - \theta$, in the third it is $\theta - 180°$, and in the fourth it is $360° - \theta$.

The exact values of lesson 3 therefore cover many more angles. The angle 210° lies in the third quadrant, so its reference angle is 30°, and its sine and cosine have the sizes of $\sin 30°$ and $\cos 30°$, namely 0.5 and 0.866, with both signs negative. Hence $\sin 210° = -0.5$ and $\cos 210° = -0.866$, as the 210° view of the figure on angles past 90° showed.

steps.headline: Find sin 210° and cos 210° from the unit circle.

workedSteps.text: The angle 210° lies between 180° and 270°, so the point is in the third quadrant, where x and y are both negative.
The reference angle is the angle past 180°.
The sizes come from 30°, whose sine is 0.5 and cosine is 0.866.
The point is below the x-axis, so the sine takes a negative sign, and the cosine is negative too.

steps.headline: Find tan 135° from the unit circle.

workedSteps.text: The angle 135° is in the second quadrant, so its reference angle is 180° − 135° = 45°.
The point is the mirror image of the one at 45°, so its sine is 0.707 and its cosine is −0.707.
Tangent is the y value divided by the x value. Work out tan 135°.

steps.headline: Adding or subtracting a full turn leaves the point where it was, and the heights of the point against the angle trace the sine wave.

lead.text: A negative angle is measured clockwise, so −60° ends at the same point as 300°, and an angle above 360° has already passed a full turn, so 400° ends where 40° does. Adding or subtracting 360° (or $2\pi$ radians) never moves the point, and so $\sin(\theta + 360°) = \sin\theta$ and $\cos(\theta + 360°) = \cos\theta$ for every angle.

Plot the height of the point against the angle and the values rise to 1 at 90°, fall through 0 at 180° to −1 at 270°, and return to 0 at 360°, and the figure shows that sine and cosine make these two waves. Their shape is the subject of the next lesson. One more fact comes from the circle itself: every point $(x, y)$ on it satisfies $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, so $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$ for every angle, which for 120° reads $(-0.5)^2 + 0.866^2 = 0.25 + 0.75 = 1$.

diagram.alt: A graph of sine against angle from 0 to 360 degrees, a wave that rises to 1 at 90 degrees, returns to 0 at 180, falls to minus 1 at 270 and returns to 0 at 360. A second view shows the cosine wave, starting at 1. In each, the value at 210 degrees is marked.
diagram.caption: The height or the sideways position of the point, plotted against the angle, traces these waves. Use the buttons to switch between sine and cosine.

reveal.text: The point ends at the same place as 40°, because 400° − 360° = 40°, so sin 400° = sin 40° = 0.643.
Both coordinates are negative, so their quotient is positive: −0.5 ÷ −0.866 ≈ 0.577, the same as tan 30°.

recap.keyIdea: On the unit circle the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), so sine and cosine exist for every angle, and a reference angle gives their size while the quadrant gives their sign.

blocks.text: You read cosine as the x value and sine as the y value of a point on the circle of radius 1, which extends both past 90° and makes their signs the signs of the coordinates. A reference angle brings any angle back to the first quadrant, and a full turn changes nothing, so every value is built from the exact values already known.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson plots the height of the moving point against the angle and reads off the repeating graph's amplitude, period and shift.

lessons.title: Graphs that repeat
lessons.orientation: Read the amplitude, period, midline and shift from a sine or cosine formula, and write a formula from a graph.
lessons.nextAction: Fit a sine or cosine model to a real cycle and use it to predict.

blocks.text: A point that goes round the unit circle at a steady speed rises and falls as it goes, and its height after turning through an angle $x$ is $\sin x$. Plotted against the angle, that height makes the wave $y = \sin x$, which stays between $-1$ and $1$ and repeats after every full turn, that is, after $2\pi$.

Tides rise and fall, daylight lengthens and shortens through the year, and a mass on a spring swings back and forth, and in each case the quantity returns to where it began after a fixed interval. Each can be described by this one wave stretched and moved to fit, so that a formula with four numbers in it records how far the quantity swings, how long a cycle takes, and the level and the moment at which it starts.

diagram.alt: The graph of y equals sine x. It rises from 0 to a maximum of 1 at pi over 2, falls to a minimum of minus 1 at 3 pi over 2, and returns to 0 at 2 pi. A second view extends it to 4 pi, showing the same shape repeating.
diagram.caption: The height of a point going round the unit circle, plotted against the angle, repeats after every full turn of 2π. Use the buttons to follow it for one turn and for two.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read amplitude, period, midline and shift from a sine or cosine formula, and write one from a graph.
intro.whyItMatters: Many repeating quantities, from tides to sound, are sine or cosine waves with four numbers to find.

reveal.text: The point completes a turn when 2x reaches 2π, which is when x reaches π. The next screen calls this length the period.

steps.headline: Four numbers describe any sine or cosine wave: the amplitude, the period, the midline and the start, and each can be read from the formula.

lead.text: Plotting the height of the point on the unit circle against the angle gives the wave $y = \sin x$, and a wave of any size, speed and position is a rescaled copy of it, written $y = A\sin\big(B(x - C)\big) + D$. The number $A$ sets the **amplitude**, the distance from the centre line up to the highest point, which is $|A|$, the size of $A$ without its sign. The number $B$ sets the **period**, the length of one full repeat, which is $\frac{2\pi}{B}$. The number $D$ sets the **midline**, the horizontal line halfway between the highest and lowest values, and $C$ is the **shift**, which slides the wave sideways.

diagram.alt: Two graphs. The first is y equals 3 sine of 2x plus 1, with y equals sine x dashed for comparison: its midline is 1, amplitude 3, period pi, maximum 4 and minimum minus 2. The second is y equals 2 cosine x minus 5, with midline minus 5, amplitude 2, period 2 pi, maximum minus 3 and minimum minus 7.
diagram.caption: Each graph is described by four numbers: the midline, the amplitude, the period and where it starts. Use the buttons to compare the two formulas.

afterFigure.text: The first graph in the figure is $y = 3\sin 2x + 1$. Its midline is $y = 1$, its amplitude is 3, so it rises to a maximum of $1 + 3 = 4$ and falls to a minimum of $1 - 3 = -2$, and its period is $\frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$, half that of $\sin x$, which is dashed for comparison. The second graph, $y = 2\cos x - 5$, has midline $-5$ and amplitude 2, so it runs between $-3$ and $-7$ and repeats every $2\pi$. In general **the maximum is $D + |A|$ and the minimum is $D - |A|$**.

steps.headline: Read the amplitude, period, midline, maximum and minimum of y = −4 sin(πx/2) + 3.

workedSteps.text: Compare the formula with A sin(Bx) + D to find the numbers.
The amplitude is the size of A. The minus sign reflects the graph, so the wave falls first, and it does not change the height of the peaks.
The period is 2π divided by B.
The midline is y = D, and the extremes lie one amplitude above and below it.

steps.headline: A shift slides the wave sideways, a minus sign flips it, and a cosine is a sine that starts a quarter turn earlier.

lead.text: Replacing $x$ by $x - C$ moves the wave to the right by $C$, since each value that used to occur at $x$ now occurs at $x + C$. The graph of $\sin(x - \frac{\pi}{3})$ is the sine wave moved right by $\frac{\pi}{3}$, so it crosses the axis upward at $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and not at 0. A negative $A$ turns the wave upside down, so $-\sin x$ falls first, yet its height is still 1.

diagram.alt: Three variations of the sine graph, each drawn with y equals sine x dashed. Sine of x minus pi over 3 is the same wave moved right by pi over 3. Minus sine x is the wave reflected, falling first with amplitude still 1. Cosine x is the sine wave moved left by pi over 2, starting at its maximum.
diagram.caption: A shift slides the wave sideways, a minus sign flips it over, and cosine is sine started a quarter turn earlier. Use the buttons to compare them.

afterFigure.text: Cosine fits the same pattern, because $\cos x$ is the sine wave moved left by $\frac{\pi}{2}$, starting at its maximum of 1. **A sine graph passes through the midline at its start, and a cosine graph starts at an extreme**, so when a cycle begins at its highest or lowest point cosine is the simpler choice, and when it begins at the midline sine is. Neither a shift nor a sign changes the amplitude.

reveal.text: The period is 2π ÷ 3 ≈ 2.094, and exactly three repeats fit into the 2π length of one repeat of sin x.

steps.headline: To write a formula from a graph, take the midline from the middle of the extremes, the amplitude from half their gap and the period from one repeat.

lead.text: The reading can be run backwards. Suppose a wave has a maximum of 9, a minimum of 1, and repeats every 8 units, starting at the midline and rising. The midline is halfway between the extremes, $D = \frac{9 + 1}{2} = 5$, and the amplitude is half the gap, $A = \frac{9 - 1}{2} = 4$. The period of 8 gives $B = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}$, and the formula is $y = 4\sin\frac{\pi x}{4} + 5$.
The same three steps work for any wave, and a check is built in: substituting a value of $x$ at which you can read the graph, such as the start, should return the value that you read.

steps.headline: A wave has a maximum of 8, a minimum of 2 and a period of 6, and it starts at its midline and rises. Write it as y = A sin(Bx) + D.

workedSteps.text: The midline is halfway between the extremes.
The amplitude is half the distance between the extremes.
The period 6 equals 2π divided by B, so B is 2π divided by 6. Give B as a decimal to three places.

steps.headline: The period and B are two ways of stating how fast a cycle repeats, and the same formulas describe waves and springs.

lead.text: A cycle that repeats $f$ times each second has a period of $T = \frac{1}{f}$ seconds, and the matching $B$ is $\frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f$. A sound of 50 cycles per second has a period of 0.02 s and a $B$ of $100\pi$, about 314 per second, so its height at time $t$ can be written $A\sin(100\pi t)$. A mass on a spring follows the same form, a cosine when it is released from its greatest stretch, which is why cosine is the usual choice there, and the amplitude is the size of the stretch.

The units of $x$ matter. With $x$ in radians the period of $\sin x$ is $2\pi$, and a formula written for degrees has a period of 360 instead, so a calculator must be in the mode that matches the formula.

reveal.text: The midline is y = 2 and the amplitude is 5, so the lowest value is 2 − 5 = −3 and the highest is 7.
B = 2π ÷ 12 = π/6 ≈ 0.524 per month, and the same extremes give D = 12 and A = 10.

recap.keyIdea: A sine or cosine wave y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D has amplitude |A|, period 2π/B, midline y = D and a start moved by C.

blocks.text: You started from the wave traced by the unit circle and saw that each of its numbers has a visible meaning. The amplitude is a distance, so a negative A only flips the wave, the period is 2π divided by B, so a larger B gives shorter repeats, and the midline lies halfway between the maximum and minimum.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson fits these four numbers to a real cycle, a Ferris wheel and then daylight and tides, and uses the model to predict.

lessons.title: Modelling cycles
lessons.orientation: Fit a sine or cosine model to a cycle, evaluate it, and solve it for a time.
lessons.nextAction: Prove the identities that always hold between sine and cosine, and use the angle-sum formulas.

blocks.text: A Ferris wheel with its centre 12 m above the ground and a radius of 10 m takes 40 s to turn once, and a rider who starts at the bottom is 2 m up at the beginning and 22 m up after a half turn. Although the wheel turns at a steady rate, the height changes quickly in some parts of the turn and slowly in others, so it cannot follow a straight line, and since the pattern repeats exactly once every 40 s, a rule that gives the height at any moment must be one of the waves of the last lesson.

Each fact about the wheel supplies one number in that wave: the centre gives the level the rider rises and falls about, the radius gives how far above and below it the rider goes, and the time for a turn gives the period. Once the rule is written down it gives the height at any chosen time, and it can be turned round to give the times at which a chosen height is passed.
